title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 139
paragraphs: I am forced here to declare an opinion that most men will find distasteful, but I will not refrain from saying what I plainly see to be the truth. If the Athenians, seized with fear of the danger threatening them, had abandoned their country, or if, without abandoning it, they had stayed and given themselves up to Xerxes, no one would have opposed the king at sea. And if no one had opposed Xerxes at sea, on land things would have gone somewhat like this: even if the Peloponnesians had thrown many rings of walls across the Isthmus, the Lacedaemonians would have been deserted by their allies — not willingly, but of necessity, since their allies would have been subdued city by city by the barbarian's fleet, and the Spartans would have been left alone. Left alone, and showing great deeds of valor, they would have died nobly. Either that, or, seeing the rest of the Greeks going over to the Medes, they would have come to terms with Xerxes before that. Either way, Greece would have fallen under Persian rule. As for the supposed benefit of walls thrown across the Isthmus, I cannot see what good they would have been once the king commanded the sea. As it is, if anyone should say that the Athenians were the saviors of Greece, he would not miss the truth. For whichever way they turned, the balance was likely to tip. They were the ones who, preferring that Greece should continue to exist in freedom, roused up all of Greece that had not already gone over to the Medes — and, after the gods at least, they were the ones who repelled the king. Not even the dreadful oracles that came from Delphi and cast them into dread induced them to abandon Greece. They stayed and endured to receive the invader into their land.
